title: “GUARD YOUR HEART” DOES NOT MEAN BUILD A WALL: THE BIBLE VERSE WE USE TO JUSTIFY HIDING
paragraphs: “GUARD YOUR HEART” DOES NOT MEAN BUILD A WALL: THE BIBLE VERSE WE USE TO JUSTIFY HIDING
Proverbs 4:23 was never permission to become cold, unreachable, suspicious, or afraid to love. What if guarding your heart means something far deeper—and far more dangerous to the darkness inside us?
“Guard your heart.”
You have probably heard those words after heartbreak.
After betrayal.
After someone you trusted turned your vulnerability into ammunition.
After the relationship you prayed over collapsed.
After the friend who knew your wounds became the person who caused another one.
After church hurt.
After abandonment.
After you finally admitted what was happening inside you and discovered that the person listening was not as safe as you thought.
So you learned something.
Or at least you thought you did.
Don’t let people get too close.
Don’t tell them everything.
Don’t love too deeply.
Don’t trust too quickly.
Keep part of yourself inaccessible.
And somewhere along the way, somebody attached a Bible verse to your survival mechanism:
“Above all else, guard your heart.”
It sounded biblical.
It felt wise.
And because pain had already taught you to retreat, the verse seemed to give your walls the voice of God.
But there is a problem.
That is not what Proverbs 4:23 is teaching.
And some of us have spent years calling something “discernment” that is actually fear wearing church clothes.
The Hebrew deserves to be heard.
Proverbs 4:23 says:
מִכָּל־מִשְׁמָר נְצֹר לִבֶּךָ כִּי־מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים
Mi-kol mishmar, netzor libbekha, ki mimmennu totze’ot chayyim.
The sense is:
“Above all guarding, guard your heart, for from it are the outgoings/springs of life.”
The word translated “guard” is connected to the Hebrew נצר (natsar)—to watch, preserve, keep, protect.
But pay attention to what is being guarded.
לֵב — lev, the heart.

To modern ears, “heart” often means primarily our emotions, especially romantic feelings. In biblical Hebrew, however, the heart reaches much deeper. It is the inner person—the center of thought, desire, intention, moral decision, understanding, and will.
That changes everything.
Solomon is not merely saying, “Protect your feelings so nobody can hurt you.”
He is warning you to watch carefully what governs the person you are becoming.
And the context makes that unmistakable.
Read the verses surrounding Proverbs 4:23.

A father is instructing his son to listen to words of wisdom. He tells him not to let those words depart from his eyes and to keep them within his heart. Then comes the command to guard the heart. Immediately afterward he speaks about corrupt speech, the direction of the eyes, the path of the feet, and turning away from evil.
Heart.
Mouth.
Eyes.
Feet.
Do you see it?
This is not principally a lesson about emotional self-defense.
It is a lesson about spiritual formation.
Guard what enters and rules the inner person because eventually the condition of the inner person appears in the direction of your life.
Jesus later exposes this reality with terrifying clarity.
In Mark 7, Christ explains that what defiles a person does not simply come from somewhere outside them.
He says:
ἔσωθεν γὰρ ἐκ τῆς καρδίας τῶν ἀνθρώπων…
esōthen gar ek tēs kardias tōn anthrōpōn…
“For from within, out of the heart of men…”
And then Jesus names what can emerge from there: evil thoughts, sexual immorality, theft, murder, adultery, greed, wickedness, deceit, sensuality, envy, slander, pride, and foolishness.
That is why guarding your heart matters.
Not because everyone outside your heart is the greatest danger.
Sometimes the enemy you desperately need God to confront is already being entertained inside it.
Bitterness.
Pride.
Lust.
Envy.
Unforgiveness.
Self-righteousness.
The craving for approval.
The secret resentment you rehearse when nobody is listening.
The fantasy you keep feeding.
The wound that has slowly become an identity.
The anger you refuse to surrender because being angry feels safer than grieving.
The relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ, but you keep renaming compromise “love.”
The applause you need so desperately that obedience feels disappointing when nobody notices.
Guarding your heart means taking seriously what is being permitted to shape you.
And this is where the verse becomes painfully personal.
You can lock everybody out and still have an unguarded heart.
You can delete someone’s number and still replay them in your imagination every night.
You can leave a toxic relationship while carrying its poison into every relationship that follows.
You can stop speaking to someone without ever forgiving them.
You can build boundaries while secretly feeding bitterness.
You can become difficult to hurt because you have become difficult to love.
You can protect yourself so successfully that eventually nobody can reach the parts of you that desperately need healing.
Even worse…
you can call the whole thing wisdom.
Biblical boundaries are real.
Discernment is biblical.
There are people you should not trust with unrestricted access to your life.

Jesus Himself did not entrust Himself indiscriminately to everyone. John 2:24 says that Jesus “did not entrust himself to them” because He knew what was in humanity. Matthew 10:16 records Him telling His disciples to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves.”
So Christianity does not demand naïveté.
Forgiveness does not automatically restore trust.
Reconciliation and restored access are not identical things.
Love does not require enabling abuse.
Grace does not mean pretending destructive behavior is harmless.
You can forgive someone and still recognize that rebuilding trust requires repentance, truth, wisdom, time, and fruit.
But there is an enormous difference between a boundary and a fortress.
A boundary says, “You cannot treat me this way.”
A fortress says, “Nobody will ever get close enough to hurt me again.”
A boundary can be governed by wisdom.
A fortress is often governed by fear.
A boundary can still love.
A fortress eventually forgets how.
And perhaps nobody knows that better than the person reading this who has whispered:
“I’m just protecting my peace.”
Maybe you are.
But ask yourself something harder.
Are you protecting peace…
or protecting an untreated wound from ever being touched?
Because those are not always the same thing.
Sometimes the wall that kept the wrong person out yesterday keeps the right people out tomorrow.
Sometimes what began as survival becomes isolation.
Sometimes what began as caution becomes cynicism.
Sometimes discernment quietly becomes suspicion.
Sometimes independence becomes an excuse to never need the Body of Christ.
Sometimes “I’m fine alone” really means:
“I cannot survive being abandoned again.”
And Jesus does not shame that wounded place.
He comes toward it.
This is the Christ who stood near graves and wept.
The Christ who allowed Himself to be moved with compassion.
The Christ who loved people knowing some would reject Him.
The Christ who washed Judas’s feet while knowing betrayal was approaching.
The Christ who entered Gethsemane and said:
“My soul is very sorrowful, even to death.”
Jesus was holy without becoming emotionally numb.
He was discerning without becoming loveless.
He was courageous without pretending pain did not hurt.
He knew betrayal was coming and still loved.

That does not mean you should imitate Judas’s access to Jesus as a formula for remaining in abusive relationships. Christ’s redemptive mission is unique, and Scripture never commands you to volunteer for mistreatment.
It means something far more beautiful:
Holiness does not require emotional deadness.
The goal of guarding your heart is not to make your heart impossible to reach.
It is to keep your heart surrendered to God.
That distinction matters.
Because a guarded heart and a hardened heart can look remarkably similar from the outside.
Both may say no.
Both may walk away.
Both may establish distance.
But one remains tender before God.
The other has decided never to feel that deeply again.
Scripture repeatedly warns not merely about wounded hearts, but hardened ones.
Hebrews 3:15 says:
Σήμερον ἐὰν τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούσητε, μὴ σκληρύνητε τὰς καρδίας ὑμῶν.
“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts.”
That should stop us.
Because you can spend so much energy guarding yourself from people that you stop noticing when you are hardening yourself toward God.
You stop confessing.
Stop trusting.
Stop expecting.
Stop praying honestly.
Stop letting anyone challenge you.
Stop receiving correction.
Stop believing restoration is possible.
Eventually the heart becomes a locked room.
And Jesus is standing at the very place you have been protecting.
Not because He wants to humiliate you.
Because He wants to heal what fear convinced you to hide.
This is where “guard your heart” becomes Gospel.
You cannot perfectly guard yourself into holiness.
You need a new heart.
The Bible’s answer to the corruption of the human heart is not merely better emotional security.
It is transformation.
God promised through Ezekiel:
“I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.”
That is Ezekiel 36:26.
Not a better wall.
A new heart.
Not emotional anesthesia.
Transformation.
Not pretending the past never happened.
Redemption.
This is why Jesus Christ must remain at the center of this conversation.
Your deepest problem is not merely that somebody broke your heart.
And your deepest hope is not merely finding someone who never will.
Our deepest problem is sin.
Theirs.
Yours.
Mine.
Sin corrupts relationships because sin corrupts people.
We hurt.
We betray.
We manipulate.
We lust.
We lie.
We worship ourselves.
We demand from human beings what only God can provide.
We turn relationships into idols and then become devastated when those idols prove mortal.
And into this wreckage comes Jesus.
Not standing at a safe distance.
Entering it.
The Son of God takes flesh.
He lives without sin.
He loves perfectly.
He is rejected.
Mocked.
Abandoned.
Betrayed.
Crucified.
And on that cross, Jesus does something your emotional walls could never accomplish.
He deals with sin.
“For our sake He made Him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21).
Then the grave receives Him.
And the grave loses.
Christ rises.
Grace walks out of the tomb.
And suddenly your story does not have to end where the scandal happened.
Your betrayal does not receive the final sentence.
Your divorce does not receive the final sentence.
Your rejection does not receive the final sentence.
Your sexual past does not receive the final sentence.
Your addiction does not receive the final sentence.
Your shame does not receive the final sentence.
Your failures do not receive the final sentence.
Even the sins you committed—not merely the sins committed against you—do not have to receive the final sentence when you come to Christ in repentance and faith.
That is the Gospel.
Not “protect yourself until nothing can hurt you.”
But:
Come to Jesus and become His.
Repent.
Believe.
Be forgiven.
Be reconciled to God.
Let Christ teach you how to love without worshiping people, forgive without enabling sin, establish boundaries without hatred, discern without paranoia, and remain tender without becoming naïve.
Maybe the prayer you need tonight is not:
“God, keep everyone from hurting me.”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, guard my heart from becoming someone I was never meant to become because somebody hurt me.”
Guard me from bitterness.
Guard me from vengeance.
Guard me from lust disguised as loneliness.
Guard me from settling because I am afraid nobody else will come.
Guard me from confusing attention with love.
Guard me from making another human being my savior.
Guard me from calling isolation peace.
Guard me from calling fear wisdom.
Guard me from weaponizing Scripture to avoid vulnerability.
Guard me from becoming proud of how little I need anyone.
Guard me from forgiving with my mouth while prosecuting them every night in my imagination.
Guard me from becoming so obsessed with what they did to me that I stop asking what You want to do in me.
And Jesus…
guard me from a heart that can recognize everybody else’s sin except my own.
That prayer is dangerous.
Because Jesus may answer it by exposing things.
He may reveal that some walls really are necessary boundaries.
He may also reveal that others are monuments to fear.
He may ask you to forgive someone who never apologized—not to declare evil acceptable, but to release vengeance into God’s hands.
He may ask you to repent to somebody you blamed entirely.
He may tell you to leave something destructive.
He may tell you to stop running from something healthy.
He may send mature believers into your life who refuse to flatter your dysfunction.
He may teach you that healing is not becoming the person you were before the wound.
Sometimes healing is allowing Christ to make you more like Himself through what you never would have chosen.
So guard your heart.
Yes.
Guard it fiercely.
But guard it biblically.
Guard what you consume.
Guard what you repeatedly imagine.
Guard what voices disciple you.
Guard what resentment you feed.
Guard what theology you believe.
Guard what entertainment trains your desires.
Guard whose approval controls your obedience.
Guard the secret compromises nobody sees.
Guard against the slow normalization of sin.
Guard against false teaching.
Guard against pride.
Guard against despair.
Guard against making pain your permanent identity.
And above everything else, keep bringing that heart beneath the Word of God and before Jesus Christ.
Because the safest heart is not the heart nobody can reach.
It is the heart Christ rules.
Maybe this article found you while you were thinking about somebody.
Maybe you immediately saw their face.
But before you send this to them, sit with it yourself.
Where have you confused guarding your heart with hardening it?
Where has pain become permission for bitterness?
Where have you used boundaries to avoid obedience?
Where have you called fear discernment?
And where have you actually lacked wise boundaries because you were afraid that saying “no” would make you unloving?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Your comment may become the sentence another wounded believer reads tonight and realizes, “I’m not the only one.”
And if somebody came into your mind while reading this, send this to them.
Because the next time pain tells you to build another wall, you may need to remember the difference between protecting your heart from corruption and protecting your heart from ever loving again.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the unbeliever who is quietly asking questions about Jesus to follow as well. The goal is not merely more religious content on a feed. It is daily Scripture, conviction, encouragement, biblical truth, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases spiritual blessing.
It cannot.
Scripture teaches no such thing.

We glorify God through lives surrendered to Christ, and one way believers may freely choose to steward what God has entrusted to them is by supporting faithful Gospel work and helping biblical truth reach others.
So if you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior keep doing this?”
Jesus is not selling you grace.
The cross cannot be purchased.
Forgiveness cannot be earned.
Salvation is not merchandise.
The invitation of Christ remains what it has always been:
Come.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Receive mercy.
Follow Jesus.

And then take whatever He has entrusted to you—your story, your resources, your voice, your influence, your scars, even the testimony formed in places you once wished had never existed—and place it back into His hands.
Because perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to understand most.
The scandal may explain the wound.
But it does not get to write the ending.
Guard your heart—but never guard it so fiercely that you lock Jesus outside the room where you hurt the most.
